# Vaporwave: neon horizon

Select `VaporwaveLoop` in the Studio. The preset `presets/vaporwave-horizon.json` creates a **16-second, 1920×1080, 60 fps** loop in MP4/WebM, meant as a stream overlay background. The composition's own initial values are `seed: 88`, `backgroundColor: #120C2E` and the classic vaporwave palette of pink, cyan, light yellow and lilac. The scene is drawn in SVG, with no text, external images, extra fonts or audio.

On screen there is an indigo night sky, with a lilac glow at the top, stars and a few four-pointed twinkles; a large sliced retro sun, from light yellow to pink and lilac, with a halo and a reflection on the ground; cyan wireframe mountain ranges, with a second, paler range behind and a distant silhouette on the horizon; a neon perspective grid floor, with pink lines and cyan columns; dark palms on the sides, with a thread of neon light only on the side facing the sun; and translucent wireframe solids (octahedron, icosahedron and pyramid) floating in the corners. The mountains' mesh follows contour lines — ridge, two intermediate levels and the foot — linked by meridians and alternating diagonals, and the faces turned to the sun get more light. No peak touches the sun's edge: a peak that would sit less than 40 px from it is pushed out of the disc, or further into it. No peak sits less than 120 px from the crown of the small palms on the horizon, so they never seem perched on a peak. The ridges fade just above the horizon, so the pink horizon line stays continuous, without cyan stretches. The sun's slices show the night sky through the disc, and the halo stops at the horizon: below it, the ground gets only the sun's flattened reflection.

The content area is the **1100×620 pixel** rectangle centered in the frame (x from 410 to 1510, y from 230 to 850). Palms, solids, twinkles and shooting stars never enter it, in any phase of the cycle and with any seed: the computation uses the drawn geometry, including the leaves' sway, the solids' float and the glow around them, and the tests check it.

The grid moves towards the camera. Each line is born transparent in a depth haze and leaves through the bottom edge, so the band near the horizon stays calm, without a pile of thin lines. The sun's cuts move down slowly, two bands per cycle, and open from zero. The palm leaves sway a few degrees, the solids make one full turn per cycle and float a few pixels, the stars and twinkles blink slowly, and the neon of the horizon and the mountains breathes. Shooting stars cross only the top band, always flying away from the sun (with the sun in the center, they pass well above it), and are invisible at the loop seam; like everything else, they repeat the same path each cycle. The mountains do not move: their geometry depends only on the seed and the sun's position.

`colors[0]` is the neon pink of the floor lines, the horizon and the haze over it, the middle of the sun, the sun's halo and reflection, the palms' light thread, the back range and the top right solid; `colors[1]` is the cyan of the floor columns, the front mountains, the other solids, the glow at the top of the sky and the halo of the stars and shooting stars; `colors[2]` is the top of the sun and half of the twinkles (the other half is white); `colors[3]` is the lilac of the sky haze, the base of the sun, the trunk rings and the faces of the mountains and solids. The third and fourth colors are optional: without `colors[2]`, the top of the sun is white; without `colors[3]`, the haze uses `colors[0]`. Colors after the fourth are ignored. Any color the Studio accepts works, like `red`, `#abc` or `rgba(255, 0, 128, 0.5)`; `backgroundColor` stays in `#RRGGBB` format and also sets the tone of the palm silhouettes.

- `speed` (0–12, integer, default `4`): grid lines that pass per cycle. More lines make the floor faster; `0` holds the floor still. The speed is constant, including at the seam: with 16 seconds and the default, a new line arrives every 4 seconds. All motion follows the cycle, so when raising `durationSeconds` raise `speed` in the same proportion to keep the floor's pace (32 s → `8`, 48 s → `12`); above 48 s the floor is slower than the default. The palms' sway, the solids' spin, the sun's cuts and the stars' blinking also stretch with the cycle. For long streams, `durationSeconds: 32` with `speed: 8` keeps the floor at the default pace and spaces the shooting star to one pass every 32 seconds.
- `sunPosition` (0.1–0.9, default `0.9`): horizontal position of the sun. At `0.9` the disc spans x from 1580 to 1980, behind the palms: it sits 70 px to the right of the content area, and the frame's edge crops 60 px of it on purpose, instead of nearly touching it; `0.1` is the mirror on the left. Near the center the sun sets: between `0.35` and `0.65` it is half set, with its center on the horizon and its top at y 544, so it only touches the last 16 px of the title band; between `0.2` and `0.35` (and between `0.65` and `0.8`) it sinks gradually. The cuts follow the visible part of the disc. The mountains open a valley under the sun, and the shooting stars fly the opposite way. The sun's side is the brightest in the frame: keep chat and alerts on the opposite side, or use `0.1` to move the sun to the left.
- `neonGlow` (0–1, default `0.7`): neon glow on the grid, the horizon, the mountains, the sun's halo and the palms' light thread.
- `starCount` (0–200, default `90`): stars in the sky. Every ten stars the sky also gets a larger four-pointed twinkle, up to 12; at `0`, the sky has no stars and no twinkles. The twinkles sit in open sky above y 230, outside the content area and away from the palm crowns, so none hides behind the sun, the mountains or the palms.
- `shootingStars` (0–3, default `1`): shooting stars per cycle, always above the content area. They repeat the same path each cycle — with the default, the same star crosses the top of the frame every 16 seconds —, so on long streams use `0`, or the 32-second recipe described under `speed`.
- `palmCount` (0–3, default `2`): palms on each side. With `1`, only the palm that leans out of the frame stays, the one with the least presence over the game's corners; `2` adds the large palm, close to the camera, that grows from the same clump and forms a V with the first; `3` adds a small palm, standing on the horizon.
- `shapeCount` (0–4, default `2`): wireframe solids. The first two sit in the top corners, between the palms and the content area; the other two, in the bottom corners.
- `centerShade` (0–1, default `0.6`): a soft plate behind the content area, shaped as a 16:9 frame. It has full strength in a 980×552 px 16:9 rectangle in the center and fades over 150 px, with rounded corners; at the corners of the content area it is still above half strength, so a camera's corners are not left uncovered.

Changing the count of one layer does not rearrange the others: each layer uses its own seed sequence. Raising stars, palms or solids keeps the ones already there; the shooting stars are redistributed along the cycle.

In MP4/GIF and in opaque WebM, `centerShade` darkens with `backgroundColor` the sky and the stars behind the content and, with less strength, the ground below the horizon. The mountains and the sun sit on top of the plate. With the sun in the center, half set below the title, the disc loses at most 10% of its opacity and 20% of its yellow top, keeping the light yellow to pink gradient; the halo, which reaches the title band, is dimmed by up to 25%. With the initial values, a white title in the central band (x from 610 to 1310, y from 470 to 560) has a median contrast of about 17.9:1, and the worst pixel stays above 12:1. In the classic preset, the median stays between 15.3:1 and 15.9:1 along the cycle, and 95% of the band's pixels stay above 8.8:1; only the top of the sun, in the last 16 px of the band, is bright. In transparent WebM there is nothing to darken; `centerShade` then partly fades the sun, the stars, the twinkles, the distant hills and the middle of the horizon line behind the content. At `1`, the horizon line stays below 10% opacity between x 800 and 1120, and the ends stay lit.

With `transparent: true` and `outputFormat: "webm"`, the sky, the top glow, the ground, the plate and the haze and glow bands that cross the whole horizon disappear; of the horizon glow, only the pools on the sides remain. Sun, stars, mountains, grid, palms and solids stay with soft alpha. The mountains are drawn together, at 45% opacity, so the game shows through them: the ranges do not add up where they overlap, and the sun, the stars and the back range do not show through the front ones. Only the front ridges are redrawn with full neon. The grid dissolves earlier towards the horizon, covering only the bottom of the frame. Near the bottom edge, where games usually show health and ammo, the grid lines passing below y 976 stay at most at 40% opacity and only regain their glow gradually up to y 912, the columns stay below half opacity and the palm trunks fade out between y 860 and 950. In MP4/GIF, every element is composited over `backgroundColor`.

To export the presets with the official profiles in [Formats](../export.md#formats):

```sh
npm run render:mp4 -- VaporwaveLoop --props presets/vaporwave-horizon.json
npm run render:mp4 -- VaporwaveLoop --props presets/vaporwave-classic.json
npm run render:webm -- VaporwaveLoop --props presets/vaporwave-alpha.json
```

Switch `render:mp4` to `render:webm` or `render:gif` for the other formats.
